nameStory: The Denticulate Longhorn Bee gets its name from two distinctive features. 'Longhorn' refers to the remarkably long antennae of the males, which can be almost as long as their entire body. 'Denticulate' means 'having small teeth,' referring to tiny tooth-like projections on parts of the bee's body that help scientists tell it apart from its many cousins.
description: The Denticulate Longhorn Bee is a medium-sized native bee that's an important pollinator in New England's late summer landscape. These fuzzy, brownish bees are about half an inch long and have a robust, somewhat rectangular build. Males sport impressively long, thread-like antennae that they wave around while flying, while females have shorter antennae but carry pollen in dense brushes of hair on their hind legs. Unlike honeybees, these are solitary bees that nest in the ground.

idTips.label: Ironweed Association
idTips.description: Look for these bees buzzing around purple ironweed flowers in late summer - this strong plant preference makes them much easier to identify than other longhorn bees

idTips.label: Male Antennae
idTips.description: Males have extraordinarily long, black antennae that extend well beyond their head and wiggle constantly as they fly - much longer than typical bees

idTips.label: Body Color
idTips.description: Overall brownish or tawny coloration with dense, soft fur that feels almost velvety if you could touch it - not the bright yellow and black stripes of many other bees

idTips.label: Flight Pattern
idTips.description: Males hover and dart erratically around flowers with their long antennae streaming behind them, creating a distinctive butterfly-like flight style

idTips.label: Pollen Baskets
idTips.description: Females carry bright purple or orange pollen in thick, bristly hair on their hind legs, creating colorful 'pollen pants' that match the flowers they're visiting

habitat: Look for Denticulate Longhorn Bees in sunny, open areas where ironweed grows abundantly - old fields, prairie edges, meadows, and roadside ditches. They prefer disturbed soils for nesting, often choosing sandy banks, trail edges, or loose garden soil. These bees are most common at lower elevations throughout New England, especially in areas that transition between woodland and open space.

seasonality.spring: Adults are not yet active - they're still developing in underground nest cells where they spent the winter as pupae.
seasonality.summer: Adults emerge in mid to late summer (July-August) and become very active, with peak activity during ironweed blooming season.
seasonality.fall: Adults remain active into early fall while ironweed and other late-season flowers are still blooming, then die off after mating and egg-laying.
seasonality.winter: No adults present - next generation overwinters as developing larvae in underground nest cells.

funFact: Male Denticulate Longhorn Bees sometimes sleep by gripping flower stems or leaves with their jaws and letting their bodies dangle in the breeze all night long, looking like tiny furry ornaments swaying in the morning dew.
confusionNotes: With nine different longhorn bee species in New England, identification can be tricky, but the Denticulate Longhorn Bee's strong preference for ironweed flowers is your best clue. Memory trick: 'Denticulate loves the purple - ironweed is their circle!'
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'longhorn bees,' these insects are not related to longhorn beetles or cattle - the name simply describes the males' unusually long antennae. Many people assume all bees live in hives, but longhorn bees are solitary, with each female digging her own nest tunnel and provisioning it alone.
compareHints: Among its longhorn bee relatives, the Denticulate Longhorn Bee is most reliably distinguished by its strong association with ironweed flowers rather than physical features alone. While the Common Longhorn Bee visits many different flowers and the Pickerelweed Longhorn Bee prefers aquatic plants, the Denticulate sticks faithfully to ironweed blooms. The Two-spotted Longhorn Bee has more distinct pale markings, while the Dark-veined Longhorn has noticeably darker wing veins.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among the nine other Melissodes species in New England, the Two-spotted Longhorn Bee is distinguished primarily by those diagnostic pale spots.
Among its Melissodes relatives, Drury's Long-horned Bee is distinguished by its rustic brown coloration and preference for a wide variety of late-season flowers.

Among its Melissodes relatives, the Dark-veined Longhorn Bee stands out for having the most conspicuous dark wing veins - while Common Longhorn Bees and Two-spotted Longhorn Bees have similar body shapes and fuzzy appearance, their wing veins are typically lighter and less noticeable.

Eastern Thistle Longhorn Bees are best distinguished from their Melissodes cousins by their timing and flower preferences - they're active later in summer than most relatives and show a strong preference for thistle flowers.
